hook: A U.S. military pilot flying over the Arabian Gulf in 2020 acquired a 'weapons quality 1 track' on a balloon-like UAP at 31,000 ft and achieved a firing solution before visually confirming the object via targeting infrared sensor.
why_it_matters: This report is notable because it documents a military crew reaching 'next to shoot' — a weapons-ready lock — on a UAP, meaning the object was tracked with sufficient precision to engage. The crew's note that it resembled UAP 'previously reported from 48FW' (48th Fighter Wing, RAF Lakenheath) suggests cross-unit pattern recognition of recurring unknowns, implying a category of balloon-like objects was being seen across multiple theaters and units. Five of six pages remain fully withheld under exemption 1.4(a), limiting what can be assessed about the full operational context.
key_findings: The UAP was described as looking 'like a balloon' and was explicitly compared to previously reported UAP from the 48th Fighter Wing, indicating cross-unit awareness of similar objects.
A 'weapons quality 1 track' was established — the highest-confidence sensor lock used to support weapons employment — demonstrating the object was tracked with precision by onboard systems.
The crew executed a 'next to shoot' on the track, meaning they achieved a firing solution, though no engagement occurred.
The UAP was visually identified through the aircraft's TFLIR (Targeting Forward-Looking Infrared), providing sensor-confirmed observation at 31,000 ft MSL.
Five of six pages are entirely withheld under classification exemption 1.4(a) (military plans, weapons systems, or operations), leaving the majority of the report's content inaccessible.

legacy_program_connections.reasoning: The official description states U.S. military MISREPs of this type are submitted directly to AARO, placing this document within AARO's active UAP intake pipeline.

As a military aeronautical UAP report involving sensor tracking and aircraft engagement systems, it fits the long-standing Air Force technical collection mission historically centered at Wright-Patterson, though no direct institutional link is named.

The balloon-like UAP description and military pilot visual/sensor report echo the format and object categories that Project Blue Book catalogued decades earlier, providing historical typological continuity.
